meta.subject: Information and Communication Technology
meta.chapterTitle: Types and components of computer systems
meta.title: Dialogue-based and gesture-based interfaces

sourceRefs.sections: 1.3 Operating systems: dialogue-based and gesture-based interfaces

objectives: Describe how a dialogue-based interface lets a person control a computer using speech
Describe how sensors or cameras detect movements in a gesture-based interface
Give examples of spoken commands and gestures used in a car or at home
Give advantages and disadvantages of both types of interface
Compare dialogue-based and gesture-based interfaces using clear differences

learn.title: What is a dialogue-based interface?
learn.body: A **dialogue-based interface** lets a person give **spoken commands** to a computer. The system recognises the speech and can carry out a task or give a spoken reply. The user does not have to press a button for every instruction.

learn.title: How a voice command is processed
items: A person speaks a question or command to a smart device.
The device changes the voice input into digital data (a binary stream).
The computer processes the instruction and chooses an action or answer.
The device can respond aloud to the person.

learn.alt: Two separate scenes: a driver speaking to an in-car navigation system and a person moving a hand near a car radio without touching it
learn.caption: Speech controls a dialogue-based interface. Movement controls a gesture-based interface.
learn.imagePrompt: Two-panel clean, friendly flat educational illustration for a school lesson. Left panel: driver sitting safely with both hands on the steering wheel, speaking toward a simple in-car navigation display, subtle sound waves. Right panel: close view of a hand making a circular finger motion near a car radio control without touching it, a small sensor visible. Clear, accurate everyday objects; soft teal and amber tones on a white background. No text, no labels, no logos, no brand names.

learn.title: Where spoken commands are useful
items: **In cars:** drivers can control entertainment or navigation while keeping their hands on the steering wheel.
**At home:** people can speak to turn lights or other electronic equipment on and off.
**Accessibility:** people who find physical controls difficult can carry out tasks using speech.
**Security:** recognising a person's voice may help identify who is speaking.

learn.title: What is a gesture-based interface?
learn.body: A **gesture-based interface** uses movements of the **hands, head or feet** as commands. A **camera or sensor** detects a movement. **Computer vision** and **image processing** can be used to recognise it, and the computer carries out the linked action. The user does not need to touch a mechanical control.

learn.title: Four car gestures to remember
items: **Rotate a finger clockwise** near the radio to turn the volume up; rotate it anticlockwise to turn the volume down.
**Separate the thumb and next finger** to change the music track.
**Move a foot underneath the rear bumper** to open the boot.
**Move a hand near the window switch** to open the window.

learn.title: From movement to action
learn.body: The camera or sensor notices the gesture and sends a **signal** to the computer. The computer works out which command the movement represents. It then performs the action, such as opening the boot. This can replace several dashboard buttons or dials.

rows.label: Input
rows.b: Movements of hands, head or feet

rows.label: How input is handled
rows.a: The system recognises speech and processes the instruction
rows.b: A sensor or camera detects movement; image processing can recognise it

rows.label: Main advantage
rows.a: A driver can keep both hands on the wheel; useful for people with disabilities
rows.b: No touch or mechanical input device is needed; movements can feel natural

rows.label: Other advantage
rows.a: A person's voice may be used for identification
rows.b: Little or no training is needed for simple gestures

rows.label: Recognition problem
rows.a: Commands may be missed or need repeating, especially with background noise
rows.b: Accidental movement may be treated as a command

rows.label: Other limit
rows.a: Setup can be complex; users need to know available commands
rows.b: The textbook gives a short detection range (about 1.5 m) and a limited set of recognised movements

learn.title: Choose the interface for the task
learn.body: A driver asks the navigation system for the nearest airport while keeping both hands on the steering wheel. This is **dialogue-based** because the command is spoken. When someone moves a foot under a car's rear bumper to open the boot, that is **gesture-based** because a movement is detected.

learn.title: Exam tip: give the reason, not only the label
learn.body: If asked to **describe** a gesture, name the movement **and** what it does: "Moving a foot under the rear bumper makes the boot open." For an **explain** question about driving, link the benefit to the driver: "Spoken commands mean the driver can keep their hands on the wheel."

learn.title: Common mistake: confusing gesture with touch
learn.body: Pressing a button is **not** a gesture-based command in the textbook examples. The gesture is detected by a camera or sensor **without touching** the control. Also, speaking a command is dialogue-based, not gesture-based.

learn.title: In real life
learn.body: Modern systems do not all have the same recognition distance or accuracy. The 1.5 m figure is the limitation stated in this textbook's comparison. For an exam question based on these pages, learn the textbook's examples and limitations.

check.prompt: A driver speaks a destination and the navigation system answers aloud. Which interface is being used?
check.hint: Focus on what the person does to send the instruction: are words said aloud, or is a physical movement detected?
check.explanation: The system receives a spoken command and can reply by voice. That is a dialogue-based interface.

check.prompt: Tick (✓) whether each statement is an advantage or a disadvantage of a dialogue-based interface.
check.hint: Decide whether each effect makes the task easier or introduces a difficulty; think about the surroundings and the person using the system.

rows.statement: A driver can keep their hands on the steering wheel.
rows.explanation: Speech avoids needing to operate a physical control.

rows.statement: Background noise may make spoken commands hard to recognise.
rows.explanation: Noise can reduce speech recognition accuracy.

rows.statement: It may help someone who finds switches difficult to use.
rows.explanation: Many tasks can be done by speech alone.

rows.statement: The user may need to learn which voice commands are available.
rows.explanation: Only supported commands can be recognised.

check.explanation: Four rows; every two correct answers earn one mark.

check.prompt: Complete the sentences with words from the list. Use each word once only.
check.hint: Think about how each interface takes its input, and what around you can stop spoken commands from working well.

items.sentence: A dialogue-based interface uses the human ___ to give commands.
A car can detect a gesture using a camera or a ___.
Background ___ can make spoken instructions hard to recognise.

check.explanation: Voice is the dialogue input; a sensor can detect gestures; noise is a limitation of speech recognition.

check.prompt: Match each car gesture to the action it causes.
check.hint: Picture each movement, then consider which part of the car or its controls the movement is meant to affect.

left.text: Rotate a finger clockwise near the radio
Move a foot beneath the rear bumper
Separate the thumb and next finger

check.explanation: These are the gestures and results listed in the textbook; the window action is the extra option.

practice.prompt: Give two uses of a dialogue-based interface. [2]

markPoints.point: Control an in-car navigation system / request directions
Control a car entertainment system / radio by voice
Switch home lights on or off using speech
Operate home electronic equipment by voice
Support a person with disabilities to carry out tasks by speech
Identify a person using their voice as a security feature

practice.modelAnswer: A driver can ask for directions using speech. At home, a person can turn the lights on by voice.
practice.explanation: Any two different uses. Name a task or context, not a device brand.

practice.prompt: Give two advantages of a dialogue-based interface. [2]

markPoints.point: Driver need not take hands off steering wheel
Useful for people with disabilities / tasks can be performed by spoken words
Voice recognition may identify a speaker for security

practice.modelAnswer: The driver can keep both hands on the steering wheel. Someone with a disability can carry out tasks using speech alone.
practice.explanation: Any two separate advantages from the textbook table.

practice.prompt: Give two disadvantages of using a gesture-based interface in a car. [2]

markPoints.point: An unintentional movement may be detected / cause an unwanted action
Works only fairly near the camera or sensor / textbook gives about 1.5 m
May recognise only a limited set of movements / requires exact gestures

practice.modelAnswer: An accidental movement may trigger a command. A gesture interface has a limited range, so the user must stay near the sensor.
practice.explanation: Any two distinct limitations; do not mix in disadvantages of speech input.

practice.prompt: Describe two different gestures used in a car and state what each gesture does. [4]

markPoints.point: Rotate a finger clockwise near the radio
...the radio volume increases / becomes louder
Rotate a finger anticlockwise near the radio
...the radio volume decreases / becomes quieter
Separate the thumb and next finger
...the music track changes
Move a foot underneath the rear bumper
accept: move a foot under the rear bumper

markPoints.point: ...the car boot opens
Move a hand near the window switch
...the car window opens

practice.modelAnswer: Rotate a finger clockwise near the radio. This increases volume. Move a foot under the rear bumper. This opens the boot.
practice.explanation: For each of two examples: one mark for the movement and one for its linked action. The action needs its matching gesture.

practice.prompt: A driver needs to change a route while driving. Explain why a dialogue-based interface could help, and why it might sometimes fail. [3]

markPoints.point: Driver can speak a new destination / route to the navigation system
...so the driver keeps hands on the steering wheel / does not need to operate controls
Road or passenger noise can prevent the spoken command being recognised

practice.modelAnswer: The driver can say the destination. This means they can keep both hands on the steering wheel. Traffic noise might stop the command being recognised.
practice.explanation: Award a point for the spoken command, a linked safety benefit, and a relevant recognition problem.

practice.prompt: Compare dialogue-based and gesture-based interfaces in two ways: the type of input and how it is recognised. [2]

markPoints.point: Dialogue uses spoken words whereas gesture uses body movements
Dialogue processes recognised speech whereas gesture uses a sensor/camera and computer vision/image processing

practice.modelAnswer: A dialogue-based interface uses voice whereas a gesture-based interface uses body movements. A dialogue system uses speech recognition whereas a gesture system uses cameras and image processing.
practice.explanation: For each comparison, both sides are needed. Write a full difference using “whereas”.

practice.prompt: A person finds it difficult to operate light switches at home. Explain why a dialogue-based interface could help them, and give one possible difficulty. [3]

markPoints.point: Person can speak to switch the lights on or off
...so they do not need to reach / press the physical switch
The command might not be recognised / may need repeating, especially with background noise
The system may be difficult or complex to set up
The person must know which spoken commands are supported

practice.modelAnswer: They can control lights by voice. This means there is no need to touch the light switch. Background noise may cause the instruction to be missed.
practice.explanation: Link the advantage to operating the lights without touching switches, and give one textbook limitation.

practice.prompt: Give two advantages of using a gesture-based interface.

markPoints.point: Replaces mechanical input devices / fewer buttons and dials needed
No physical contact / touch is needed
Natural way for a human to give commands
No training needed to use it

practice.modelAnswer: No physical contact is needed to give a command. It replaces mechanical controls such as buttons and dials.
practice.explanation: Any two valid points. The textbook lists: replaces mechanical input devices, no physical contact, natural for humans, no training needed.

summary: Dialogue-based interfaces use spoken commands; the system processes speech and may give a spoken reply.
Voice commands can control navigation, entertainment and home devices; they may also help with accessibility or security.
Speech input can fail because of noise, complex setup or unfamiliar commands.
Gesture-based interfaces detect hand, head or foot movements with cameras or sensors and can use image processing.
Gestures do not need touch, but accidental movements, limited range and limited recognised actions can cause problems.

flashcards.back: An interface that lets a person give spoken commands to a computer.

flashcards.front: What does a voice-command system do with speech?
flashcards.back: It converts the input to digital data, processes the instruction and can reply aloud.

flashcards.front: Give two advantages of dialogue-based interfaces.
flashcards.back: Drivers keep their hands on the wheel; people with disabilities may control devices through speech.
A camera or sensor; computer vision and image processing can recognise the movement.

flashcards.front: Which car gesture can open the boot?
flashcards.back: Moving a foot under the rear bumper.

flashcards.front: Give two limitations of gesture-based interfaces.
flashcards.back: They may detect unintended movements and may work only near the camera or sensor.
